subject: surgery
title: Intracranial neoplasms, glioblastoma multiforme, meningioma, and maximal safe resection

steps.tx: Secondary brain metastases represent the most frequent intracranial **neoplasms** in adult patients, originating predominantly from primary carcinomas of the lung, breast, skin melanoma, kidney, and colon. Among primary brain tumors, glioblastoma represents the most common and aggressive malignant histological subtype. Histopathological hallmarks include dense nuclear pleomorphism, microvascular endothelial proliferation, and prominent pseudopalisading geographic necrosis. Mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase define distinct molecular prognostic subgroups, with IDH-wildtype conferring worse clinical outcomes.
steps.say: Metastatic brain tumors from lung, breast, and melanoma are the most common adult intracranial neoplasms. Glioblastoma is the most frequent primary malignant brain tumor, characterized histologically by pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation.

rows: Antoni A & Antoni B spindle cells

steps.tx: This figure contrasts an infiltrative **glioblastoma** with a well-circumscribed meningioma. The left brain shows ill defined growth with necrosis and abnormal vessels, while the right shows a dural based mass with psammoma bodies. Microscopy pairs pseudopalisading necrosis and vascular proliferation on one side with psammoma bodies on the other. Surgery uses fluorescence guidance and awake mapping near eloquent cortex, followed by combined radiation with **temozolomide**.
steps.say: Compare the two brains and state which tumour infiltrates and which displaces. Match each microscopic feature to its tumour and explain why one recurs at the margin. Describe how fluorescence guidance and awake mapping extend a safe resection, then give the two arms of postoperative therapy and the methylation marker that predicts benefit.

vis.alt: Infiltrative glioblastoma with necrosis and vascular proliferation contrasted with a well-circumscribed, dural-based meningioma with psammoma bodies, plus Stupp protocol and mapping tools.
vis.caption: Glioblastoma versus meningioma with Stupp protocol and surgical adjuncts.

steps.tx: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap **cells** of the leptomeninges, representing the most common benign extra-axial intracranial tumor. They demonstrate a characteristic dural tail of enhancement on contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging and contain laminated calcified psammoma bodies microscopically. Vestibular schwannomas develop from the Schwann cell sheath of the inferior vestibular nerve within the internal auditory canal, producing progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, with bilateral lesions serving as the pathognomonic hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2.
steps.say: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells, presenting as extra-axial masses with a characteristic dural tail on MRI. Vestibular schwannomas arise from the vestibular nerve, producing progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

nodes.label: New onset focal deficit or seizure

steps.tx: Patients present clinically with generalized features of raised intracranial **pressure** including morning headaches, nausea, projectile vomiting, and bilateral papilledema, alongside focal neurological deficits or new-onset adult epileptic seizures. Magnetic resonance imaging with intravenous gadolinium contrast constitutes the definitive imaging modality of choice. High-grade gliomas display intense peripheral rim enhancement with central non-enhancing necrosis and extensive finger-like vasogenic edema spreading through the white matter while sparing the overlying cortex. Glioblastoma often crosses the corpus callosum in a butterfly pattern.
steps.say: Brain tumors present with morning headaches, vomiting, papilledema, and seizures. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the imaging modality of choice, displaying peripheral rim enhancement and central necrosis in glioblastomas, while tissue diagnosis is definitive.

vis.alt: Illustration of a butterfly glioblastoma crossing the corpus callosum with central necrosis and surrounding oedema.
vis.caption: Butterfly glioblastoma: irregular enhancement with central necrosis and vasogenic oedema crossing the corpus callosum. The drawing is an illustration, not a gadolinium MRI, and does not show papilloedema or fundoscopy. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: The cornerstone of surgical management is maximal safe **resection**, utilizing stereotactic neuronavigation incorporating preoperative functional MRI and tractography, intraoperative imaging, and awake craniotomy with cortical mapping when tumors abut eloquent motor or language cortex. Oral 5-aminolevulinic acid facilitates intraoperative fluorescence-guided visualization of infiltrating tumor margins under blue light. For glioblastoma, the Stupp protocol following surgical debulking combines fractionated focal external beam radiation with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide chemotherapy, yielding superior survival when the MGMT promoter is methylated.
steps.say: Maximal safe surgical resection utilizing neuronavigation and awake mapping provides the foundation of care. Glioblastoma is treated adjuvantly with the Stupp protocol of radiation and temozolomide chemotherapy.
